app.name: REDCAIRN
app.tagline: Tactical surface navigation for crewed Mars EVAs

site.name: Boxwork Terrain
site.locality: Lower Aeolis Mons (Mount Sharp), Gale crater
site.crs: IAU Mars 2000 geographic (EPSG:104905), planetocentric latitude, east-positive longitude
rationale: Gale crater was put forward three separate times as a human Exploration Zone at the 2015 human landing site workshop.
It is the only place on Mars with a 1 m orbital elevation model, 25 cm orbital imagery, 14 years of surface radiation measurements and a rover-driven track all covering the same ground.
The boxwork ridges are mineral-cemented fracture networks left by ancient groundwater, found nowhere else on the mountain, and the science team's open question is why they hardened only here.
The corridor climbs 77 m in 1.5 km across a geologic contact, so slope, mineral targets and walk-back distance all matter on a single EVA.

elevationService.note: GET only; sends no CORS header, so sample at build time and ship the result as static data.

validation.method: Orbital DEM compared with rover localisation at 324 points along the EVA route

minerals.label: Mineral / science targets
minerals.status: live: waypoint and unit annotations from surface findings
minerals.note: Orbital spectrometer footprints (CRISM, about 18 m per pixel) are too coarse for a 1.5 km walk, so targets here are tied to what the rover measured on the ground.

units.label: Boxwork terrain
units.summary: Low ridges enclosing sandy hollows, in a layer rich in magnesium sulfates. Bedrock between the ridges carries white calcium sulfate veins.

units.label: Layered sulfate unit
units.summary: Layered sulfate-bearing bedrock above the boxwork terrain. The same unit was last sampled about 160 m lower on the mountain.

eva.name: Boxwork to Sulfate Contact
eva.basis: Follows ground driven by the Curiosity rover between mission sols 4560 and 4868, with the rover's spurs and back-tracks removed.

waypoints.name: Altadena Staging

science.headline: Edge of the boxwork terrain
science.why: Bedrock at the edge of the boxwork, drilled here in June 2025 as the mission's 43rd drill hole. It gives the baseline to compare against rock inside the ridge network.
tasks: Photograph the old drill hole for change detection

pov.caption: Fractured bedrock and sand looking out from the staging point.

waypoints.story: The rover team saved the name Altadena for a special target. It is the neighbourhood beside their lab that burned in the Eaton Fire, a few months before this hole was drilled. Your walk starts at a place named for home.

waypoints.name: Ridge Ascent

science.headline: Steepest ground on the route
science.why: The rover recorded a 17° tilt at this stop and the orbital model shows 14.9° on the approach, just under the caution limit. It is the pace and footing check before the ridge network.
tasks: Photograph the ridge flank in cross-section

pov.caption: Sloping bedrock on the climb toward the first ridges.

model.alt: Terrain cross-section of the ridge flank

waypoints.story: On sol 4600 the rover tilted 17 degrees here and kept going. This is where you learn how the suit handles a real Martian slope, while the dock is still seven minutes behind you.

waypoints.name: Monte Grande

science.headline: Paired hollow and ridge samples
science.why: A ridge top and the hollow floor beside it sit about 10 m apart with 2 m of relief. Sampling both tests what cemented the ridges and left the hollows to erode. The rover found fine veins in both, with bright white and grey vein fill.
tasks: Sample white and grey vein fill separately

pov.caption: Ridge bedrock in the foreground with the sandy Monte Grande hollow behind it.

model.alt: Cross-section through a boxwork ridge and hollow

waypoints.story: Two drill holes ten metres apart, with two metres of height between them. The team named the low one for a desert valley and the high one for the tallest peak in Bolivia. “Go big or go home,” they wrote.

waypoints.name: Southern Ridges

science.headline: Layered ridges at the southern reaches
science.why: The southern end of the boxwork terrain, where the rover imaged ridges and stepped ledges on its way to the contact. Good exposure for mapping how ridge layering changes toward the boundary.
tasks: Grab sample from an exposed ledge

pov.caption: Stepped, layered ledges in the southern boxwork.

waypoints.story: The rover spent its last week in the boxwork here, photographing ridge after ridge before it left them for good. You get to put a hand on one.

waypoints.name: Southern Contact

science.headline: Where boxwork meets layered sulfate
science.why: The rover crossed the southern boundary of the boxwork terrain here. A contact is where two rock units can be sampled within arm's reach, which pins down their order and the conditions that changed between them.
tasks: Sample both sides of the contact

pov.caption: Platy bedrock slabs and sand just past the boxwork boundary.

waypoints.story: One drive in March 2026 carried the rover across this line. The team titled that week’s log “Bye-Bye Boxwork.” It crossed in a single drive. You can stop and stand with a boot on each side.

waypoints.name: Atacama

science.headline: Layered sulfate bedrock, turnaround point
science.why: First layered-sulfate bedrock above the boxwork, drilled by the rover in April 2026 and again nearby at Campo Marte. It sits about 160 m above the last sample of the same unit, so it records how the unit changes with height. Rocks here show polygonal fractures and fine lamination, and the layered Paniri butte is in view.

pov.caption: Polygon-textured bedrock slabs separated by sand at the Atacama site.

waypoints.story: Turnaround. The rover drilled twice here, and the same rock was last sampled 160 metres below you. Look back down the slope: the whole walk is in view, and the way home is already marked.

suit.note: Planning assumptions for the demo, not flight values. Each one is editable and labelled as simulated in the app.

speed.formula: kmh = suitFactor * baseKmh * exp(-k * abs(tan(slope) + offset))

suit.walkBackRule: Consumables remaining must always cover the walk back to the dock at current pace, plus the oxygen reserve.

radiation.backgroundBasis: Average galactic cosmic ray dose equivalent measured on the surface at Gale crater by the rover's radiation detector.
radiation.careerLimitNote: Agency career limit adopted in 2022; confirm the figure before quoting it in the presentation.

terrainShielding.basis: Measured while the rover was parked at the foot of a cliff at Murray Buttes, 9–21 September 2016.
terrainShielding.model: Dose reduction = efficiency x fraction of sky hidden by terrain, scanned in 16 directions out to 80 m on the elevation grid.
terrainShielding.efficiencyNote: Assumption. Blocking sky does not remove ground-scattered particles, so only half the blocked fraction is credited.
candidates: Paniri butte (near WP5; to be located on the HiRISE mosaic)

scenarios.label: Solar particle event
scenarios.basis: Shaped on the September 2017 event, when surface radiation at Gale roughly doubled; later analysis put the peak near three times background.
scenarios.demoSeverityNote: Exaggerated on purpose so the reroute logic is visible in a short demo. Shown as simulated.
scenarios.response: Recalculate the fastest safe return to the dock and flag terrain shielding on the way.

scenarios.label: Dust storm
scenarios.basis: Rising atmospheric dust cuts visibility and solar power. Opacity values are demo assumptions.
scenarios.response: Reduce pace, tighten the walk-back margin and recommend return before visibility drops below waypoint spacing.

briefing.kicker: EVA-01 · Gale crater · Lower Mount Sharp
briefing.title: A rover walked this ground alone so that you would not have to.
body: For fourteen years one machine climbed this mountain at a few metres a day. Every place it stopped, it left a record: where it stood, how far it tilted, what the rock was made of, what the sky was doing.

On Earth, hikers stack stones into cairns to mark the safe way for whoever comes next. REDCAIRN turns the rover's stops into cairns. This is the first trail on Mars a person can follow out, and follow home.

anchorResources.name: Mars Trek
anchorResources.role: Every map pixel and every elevation value: the 25 cm orbital mosaic, the 1 m elevation model behind slope, routing, shielding and the 3D terrain blocks, and the human Exploration Zones layer behind the site choice.

anchorResources.name: USGS planetary geologic mapping
anchorResources.role: The regional unit under the whole walk, read from the global geologic map at the site: Htu, the Hesperian transition undivided unit.

anchorResources.name: Curiosity's proposed path up Mount Sharp
anchorResources.role: The plan this walk completes. That map promised a climb from clay through sulfate-bearing rock; the EVA follows the track the rover actually drove through the sulfate unit.

anchorResources.name: Worldview
anchorResources.role: The model for the layer stack, and the link home: each waypoint named after a place on Earth opens that place in Worldview.

anchorResources.name: Perseverance raw images
anchorResources.role: A live feed of the newest frame from the other rover, at Jezero crater, shown in the briefing and this panel. The same image service family supplies the eye-level photos at each waypoint.
